ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee.
In each trial, participants were asked to predict whether a child protagonist would seek help from a familiar teacher or an unfamiliar teacher who displayed either a positive or a negative response.
Forty-five Han Chinese children aged 5-6 years (range = 5.17-6.17 years, M = 5.81, SD = 0.28, 22 boys) were recruited from two preschools in Hangzhou, an eastern city in P. R.
Written informed consent was obtained from the children's guardians, and oral assent was obtained from the participants.
At the beginning of the task, participants were introduced to a child protagonist and two teacher figures (see Figure 1).
table.formatted: At the beginning of the task, participants were introduced to a child protagonist and two teacher figures (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

table.text: After hearing the story, participants were asked to predict whether the child protagonist would seek help from the teacher.

Based on the sample size calculation from Study 1, an additional 45 Han Chinese children aged 4-7 years (range = 4.58-7.08 years, M = 6.24; SD = 0.68, 23 boys) were recruited from the same two preschools in Hangzhou, China.
Written informed consent was obtained from participants' guardians, and oral consent was obtained from all the children.

At the beginning of the task, participants were introduced to two cartoon teachers and were told which figure represented the child protagonist's familiar teacher (e.g., "This is the teacher who has been with the child since the first year of preschool") and which represented an unfamiliar teacher (i.e., "This is a teacher from another preschool whom the child has never met").
To ensure comprehension, participants were then asked to recall which teacher was familiar and which was unfamiliar.

To ensure comprehension, participants were then asked to recall which teacher was familiar and which was unfamiliar.

text.text: Effective help-seeking is essential for young children's adaptation in early childhood education settings, yet little is known about how they selectively seek help based on different social cues.
This study examined how young children integrate teachers' familiarity and response valence when predicting a protagonist's help-seeking behavior.
Across two studies, 90 Han Chinese children aged 4-6 years (45 boys) completed a third-party task simulating teacher-child interactions.
In Study 1, familiarity was manipulated using photographs of each child's real teachers, whereas Study 2 employed standardized cartoon figures and verbal cues to indicate familiarity.
The results showed that children tended to expect that the protagonist would seek help from familiar teachers, especially those who responded positively.
Meanwhile, they hesitated to expect that the protagonist would seek help from unfamiliar teachers, regardless of their response valence.
This pattern indicates that familiarity consistently exerted a stronger influence than response valence, as children consistently prioritized familiarity when anticipating support.

Together, these findings highlight how young children flexibly integrate multiple social cues when forming help-seeking expectations and offer practical implications for fostering secure, responsive teacher-child relationships in early education.

text.text: Such models help children anticipate whether adults will respond helpfully when they are in need.
Previous studies have shown that caregivers' responsiveness shapes young children's expectations about support (Jia, Shen, Fang et al., 2024; Jia, Zhou et al., 2023).

text.text: However, it remains unclear how these expectations are constructed within teacher-child interactions, where multiple social cues must be evaluated simultaneously.

The present study, therefore, focused on the process of social-cognitive integration, examining how young children combine relational (i.e., familiarity) and behavioral (i.e., response valence) information to form help-seeking expectations in early educational contexts.
Teachers' familiarity plays an important role in shaping young children's interactions within teacher-child relationships.
Familiarity provides the foundation for high-quality care and supportive engagement, fostering a sense of security and emotional comfort (Datler et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Familiarity provides the foundation for high-quality care and supportive engagement, fostering a sense of security and emotional comfort <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Datler et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical studies show that young children are more likely to seek assistance from familiar teachers, as repeated interactions with known adults reduce uncertainty and promote approach behaviors (Corriveau & Harris, 2009).

text.text: This tendency reflects young children's reliance on relational cues to guide social reasoning during early development.
Beyond familiarity, the valence of teachers' responses, whether positive or negative, also influences children's help-seeking expectations.

According to the Teaching Through Interactions framework, positive emotional climates characterized by warm, supportive responses enhance engagement and encourage help-seeking (Hamre, 2014; Hamre & Pianta, 2007).

text.text: Conversely, negative or dismissive responses can undermine children's expectations of support, discouraging future help-seeking (Jia, Wu et al., 2023).

text.text: Together, these findings highlight the importance of teachers' emotional responsiveness in guiding young children's expectations of teacher support within ECE settings.
However, in everyday classrooms, social situations rarely involve a single clear cue.
Children often face ambiguous or conflicting signals.
For example, a familiar teacher who responds negatively, or an unfamiliar teacher who responds positively.
Interpreting such mixed cues requires advanced social-cognitive processing, as children must evaluate and weigh multiple dimensions of information when anticipating others' support.

By around 5 to 6 years of age, children begin to show increasing sophistication in integrating multiple social cues when reasoning about others' behavior (Corriveau & Harris, 2009; Corriveau et al., 2009; Williams & Danovitch, 2019).

text.text: For example, Corriveau and Harris (2009) found that while younger children (aged 3-4 years) mainly relied on familiarity, 5-year-olds flexibly prioritized informant accuracy over familiarity when evaluating knowledge sources.

text.text: These findings suggest that children at this age can balance competing cues and adjust their expectations accordingly.

However, most previous studies of cue integration have focused on selective social learning contexts, in which children evaluate the accuracy of others' knowledge, rather than supportive situations that involve emotional or instrumental assistance (Corriveau & Harris, 2009; Williams & Danovitch, 2019).

text.text: Moreover, these studies often use decontextualized, low-stakes paradigms, which limit ecological validity.
To address these limitations, the present study introduces a third-party help-seeking expectation task that simulates realistic teacher-child interactions.
This paradigm allows for a direct examination of how children weigh familiarity and response valence cues when anticipating supportive behavior.

By situating these judgments within emotionally meaningful scenarios, the study provides a new perspective on the development of social cue integration and the early formation of interpersonal expectations in ECE settings.
The current study examined how young children integrate teachers' familiarity and response valence when forming help-seeking expectations.
To achieve this, we employed a third-party expectation task that simulated everyday teacher-child interactions.
In each trial, participants were asked to predict whether a child protagonist would seek help from a familiar teacher or an unfamiliar teacher who displayed either a positive or a negative response.
Teachers' response valence was manipulated through facial expressions and tone of voice.
Specifically, positive responses featured a smiling face and a warm tone, whereas negative responses showed an angry face and a disapproving tone.
To enhance ecological validity, Study 1 used photographs of real teachers.
Each participant's own lead teacher served as the familiar teacher.
Study 2 followed the same task structure but replaced real teachers with cartoon figures and conveyed familiarity verbally through the experimenter.

This modification allowed us to examine whether the effects of familiarity and response valence would remain consistent when familiarity was presented symbolically rather than based on direct experience.
We examined three main hypotheses.

First, we hypothesized that young children would predict higher help-seeking toward familiar than unfamiliar teachers based on previous findings (Corriveau & Harris, 2009; Jia, Shen, Zhu et al., 2024).

text.text: Second, drawing on evidence that preschoolers anticipate greater support from responsive caregivers (Jia, Wu et al., 2023), we predicted higher expectations toward teachers displaying positive rather than negative responses.

text.text: The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee.
Written informed consent was obtained from the children's guardians, and oral assent was obtained from the participants.
To manipulate teacher familiarity and response valence, we developed customized visual and auditory stimuli for each participant.

In the familiar condition, a photograph of each child's own lead teacher was presented; in the unfamiliar condition, a photograph of a female research assistant who was unknown to the participants was used.
All photographs were taken under standardized conditions (white background, consistent lighting) and were edited to ensure uniform brightness, hue, and vibrance.
Each teacher's face was combined onto an identical female cartoon body to maintain consistency in clothing and posture.
Response valence was manipulated through both facial expression and speaking tone.

Positive responses featured smiling faces with crescent eyebrows and warm, friendly tones, whereas negative responses featured angry faces with slightly raised (10 degrees) eyebrows and disapproving tones.

These auditory stimuli were pretested with 34 undergraduate students majoring in early childhood education, confirming a significant perceived difference between positive (M = 4.24, SD = 1.05) and negative tones (M = 1.85, SD = 0.99) on a 5-point Likert scale (t (33) = 9.40, p < .001, Cohen's d = 2.35).

text.text: All teachers depicted in the stimuli were female, ensuring both methodological control and ecological validity.
In China, the ECE workforce is predominantly female, with women accounting for 97.78% of all full-time teachers in 2020 (Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China, 2021).
Using only female teacher images thus reflected real classroom demographics and avoided gender-related confounds.
A computerized help-seeking expectation task was created in PsychoPy 3 (Peirce et al., 2022).

text.text: The task followed a 2 (familiarity: familiar vs. unfamiliar) × 2 (response valence: positive vs. negative) within-subjects design, resulting in four conditions.

Each condition included four randomized scenarios depicting common preschool challenges: (1) difficulty in doing origami, (2) inability to cut paper shapes, (3) conflict during block play, and (4) conflict while reading a picture book.
At the beginning of the task, participants were introduced to a child protagonist and two teacher figures (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: At the beginning of the task, participants were introduced to a child protagonist and two teacher figures (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: They were told that one teacher had taught the child protagonist since the first year of preschool (familiar teacher), while the other worked at a different preschool and had never met the child (unfamiliar teacher).
The position of the two teachers was counterbalanced across participants.
Each condition included four trials presented in random order.
In each trial, the child protagonist encountered a problem and cried, accompanied by a 1.5-second audio clip of a real child's cry.
A teacher then appeared from the bottom right corner of the screen and stopped on the right side.
Meanwhile, the experimenter narrated the scenario.
For example, in the familiar-positive condition, the experimenter said, "This child is trying to fold a small frog but cannot and cries sadly.
Then, their teacher comes over and asks 'What happened?' gently."
After hearing the story, participants were asked to predict whether the child protagonist would seek help from the teacher.
If they expected the child to seek help, the response was coded as a "1"; otherwise, it was coded as "0".
The order of conditions was counterbalanced across participants.
Each child completed the task individually in a quiet room within their preschool.
Upon completion, children received stickers as small rewards.

The results indicate that within ECE settings, young children tended to expect help from familiar teachers, particularly when those teachers displayed positive responsiveness.
This pattern underscores the important role of familiarity and perceived responsiveness in shaping children's expectations of social support.

Although positive responsiveness from unfamiliar teachers modestly increased children's help-seeking expectations, they remained generally reluctant to anticipate help-seeking from unfamiliar figures.
This finding highlights the enduring influence of familiarity as a primary social cue in young children's social reasoning about whom to approach for help.

These results were in line with our hypotheses and consistent with previous research showing that young children anticipate greater support from familiar and responsive caregivers than from unfamiliar or negatively responsive individuals (Jia, Shen, Zhu et al., 2024; Jia, Zhou et al., 2023).

text.text: Extending these findings, the present study found that by 5 to 6 years of age, children are capable of evaluating and integrating multiple social cues simultaneously when forming help-seeking expectations, reflecting emerging flexibility in their social-cognitive processing.
The results of Study 1 showed that young children could integrate teachers' familiarity and response valence when forming help-seeking expectations in ECE settings.
Study 2 was designed to test the robustness and generalizability of these findings while addressing potential confounds.
Specifically, we replaced real teacher photographs with cartoon teacher figures to control for the possible influence of participants' direct interpersonal experiences with their own teachers.
In this way, Study 2 examined whether children could apply the same cue-integration processes when familiarity was conveyed symbolically rather than experientially.

To ensure that familiarity cues were understood purely as communicated social information, the experimenter provided explicit verbal descriptions of whether each teacher was familiar or unfamiliar to the child protagonist.
This design allowed us to assess whether children's help-seeking expectations were grounded in their interpretation of social cues, independent of any prior personal relationships.

The participant age range was slightly broader than in Study 1, reflecting the natural age composition of the participating classrooms.
Written informed consent was obtained from participants' guardians, and oral consent was obtained from all the children.
The overall task structure in Study 2 was identical to that of Study 1, except for the presentation of teacher stimuli.
Instead of photographs of real teachers, standardized cartoon teacher figures were used to depict the familiar and unfamiliar teachers (see Figure 3).

To ensure comprehension, participants were then asked to recall which teacher was familiar and which was unfamiliar.
If their responses were incorrect, the experimenter repeated the explanation until the child demonstrated clear understanding.

text.text: Across two studies, we found that children aged 5-6 years integrated teachers' familiarity and response valence when forming help-seeking expectations in ECE settings.

Consistently, they expected that the protagonist would be most likely to seek help from familiar teachers who responded positively and least likely to seek help from unfamiliar teachers who responded negatively.
These patterns, replicated across both studies, confirm the robust influence of familiarity and response valence on young children's social expectations.
Notably, familiarity exerted a stronger influence, as children continued to expect support from familiar teachers even following negative responses.
These findings highlight young children's capacity to process multiple social cues and their pronounced tendency to prioritize relationship-based information when navigating supportive interactions.

Our results extend previous research by showing that familiarity is not merely a basis of informational trust (Danovitch & Mills, 2014; Reyes-Jaquez & Echols, 2013; Schieler et al., 2018) but a central factor of support expectations in problem-solving situations.
text.formatted: Our results extend previous research by showing that familiarity is not merely a basis of informational trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Danovitch & Mills, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Reyes-Jaquez & Echols, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Schieler et al., 2018)</ref> but a central factor of support expectations in problem-solving situations.

text.text: Previous studies suggested that children's trust in familiar adults might arise from generalized beliefs that teachers are reliable help providers (Corriveau & Harris, 2009).
text.formatted: Previous studies suggested that children's trust in familiar adults might arise from generalized beliefs that teachers are reliable help providers <ref type="bibr">(Corriveau & Harris, 2009</ref>).

text.text: Yet, our results do not support this assumption.
Even when unfamiliar teachers responded positively, children did not show higher help-seeking expectations toward them.
This pattern indicates that the social role of "teacher" alone is insufficient to elicit expectations of support.
Instead, an established interaction history is crucial for shaping help-seeking expectations in early childhood.
Our findings also show that the strength of the familiarity effect depends on how familiarity is represented.
When grounded in daily interactions (Study 1), familiarity exerted stronger effects than when conveyed symbolically through verbal information (Study 2).
The cross-study analysis confirmed this pattern.
Specifically, children relied on familiarity cues across both studies, but overall help-seeking expectations were lower when teachers were represented by cartoon figures accompanied by verbal cues.
This difference may reflect reduced experiential salience, as familiarity remained the dominant cue, but its influence weakened when direct experience was absent.
Furthermore, our results suggest that young children flexibly integrate social cues rather than following fixed rules.

In contrast to selective trust paradigms where the effects of behavioral accuracy can override familiarity (Corriveau & Harris, 2009), familiarity in our study remained a powerful predictor even under negative response conditions.
text.formatted: In contrast to selective trust paradigms where the effects of behavioral accuracy can override familiarity <ref type="bibr">(Corriveau & Harris, 2009)</ref>, familiarity in our study remained a powerful predictor even under negative response conditions.

text.text: This suggests that strong relational priors built through repeated positive teacher-child interactions may buffer the effects of short-term negative cues.

Children's expectations are therefore not purely reactive to immediate behavior but are guided by stable, experience-based representations that support adaptive help-seeking in everyday social environments.
Two complementary mechanisms may explain how children integrate familiarity and response valence when forming help-seeking expectations.
One possibility is a sequential process, in which children first assess familiarity and then evaluate responsiveness.
Unfamiliar teachers may trigger early disengagement due to perceived social risk (Gu et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Unfamiliar teachers may trigger early disengagement due to perceived social risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gu et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, children may engage in parallel integration, processing both cues simultaneously but weighting them differently according to the situation.

Evidence from selective trust research supports this latter view, showing that children as young as 4 or 5 years can coordinate perceptual and relational cues simultaneously when making social reasoning (Corriveau et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Evidence from selective trust research supports this latter view, showing that children as young as 4 or 5 years can coordinate perceptual and relational cues simultaneously when making social reasoning <ref type="bibr">(Corriveau et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings are consistent with this parallel integration account, showing that familiarity generally carried more weight, although its influence was weaker when represented symbolically rather than experienced directly, as in Study 2.

This pattern suggests that the richness of prior interaction experience modulates how children combine social information, a mechanism extending beyond informational trust to emotionally grounded supportive interactions.
Differences between the two studies further clarify this mechanism.
Children in Study 1 generally showed higher help-seeking expectations than those in Study 2.
This pattern was particularly visible in the negative response conditions, though the interaction was not statistically significant.
This contrast likely reflects experience-based versus knowledge-based representations (Dykas & Cassidy, 2011).
text.formatted: This contrast likely reflects experience-based versus knowledge-based representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dykas & Cassidy, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Photographs of real teachers in Study 1 may have activated children's episodic memories and well-established relational schemas, sustaining positive expectations even after negative cues (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016).
text.formatted: Photographs of real teachers in Study 1 may have activated children's episodic memories and well-established relational schemas, sustaining positive expectations even after negative cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the abstract, verbally conveyed familiarity in Study 2 lacked experiential depth, making children's expectations more sensitive to immediate response valence.

Together, these results indicate that not all familiarity cues are equivalent; direct relational experience provides affective and mnemonic grounding that strengthens children's confidence in social support.
Most importantly, our study moves beyond simply adapting help-seeking paradigms to new contexts.

It provides a theoretically grounded account of how familiarity depth and response valence jointly shape social expectation, linking developmental mechanisms of cue integration with applied understanding of teacher-child relationships in early education.
Our findings also contribute to theoretical refinement with attachment and social expectation frameworks.

Building on hierarchical models of attachment representations (Fraley, 2007; Waters & Waters, 2006), our results suggest that children flexibly draw on both specific representations (formed through direct interactions with a teacher) and generalized representations (derived from broader social expectations).
text.formatted: Building on hierarchical models of attachment representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fraley, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Waters & Waters, 2006)</ref>, our results suggest that children flexibly draw on both specific representations (formed through direct interactions with a teacher) and generalized representations (derived from broader social expectations).

text.text: Rather than relying on fixed schemas, children dynamically integrate these levels of representation when anticipating supportive behavior.
This dynamic integration may mark a developmental advance of the ability to flexibly weigh relational and behavioral cues when predicting others' responsiveness.

From a methodological perspective, the present study advances ongoing debates about stimulus realism in developmental research (Packer & Moreno-Dulcey, 2022 , 2023; Paulus & Caporaso, 2024; Wellman & Yu, 2022).
text.formatted: From a methodological perspective, the present study advances ongoing debates about stimulus realism in developmental research <ref type="bibr">(Packer & Moreno-Dulcey, 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Paulus & Caporaso, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wellman & Yu, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent effects across both photo-based and cartoon-based paradigms confirm the robustness of the findings, while differences in magnitude highlight how stimulus format influences the activation of relational representations.

Photo-based stimuli engage lived social experiences and elicit more ecologically grounded judgments, whereas simplified or symbolic stimuli provide experimental control but may attenuate affective engagement.

These results argue for the value of multi-method approaches that integrate ecological validity with experimental rigor, allowing researchers to triangulate findings across representational levels of social cognition.
Practically, the findings carry important implications for early education.
They highlight the important role of familiarity and consistent positive responsiveness in supporting children's adaptive help-seeking behaviors.

For educators, this underscores the importance of establishing and maintaining trusting relationships, particularly during transitional periods such as preschool entry or classroom reassignment (Howes & Ritchie, 2002).
text.formatted: For educators, this underscores the importance of establishing and maintaining trusting relationships, particularly during transitional periods such as preschool entry or classroom reassignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Howes & Ritchie, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Ensuring continuity in teacher assignments and fostering warm, responsive interactions can encourage children to seek assistance when facing challenges, thereby enhancing both emotional security and problem-solving capacity (Birch & Ladd, 1997).
text.formatted: Ensuring continuity in teacher assignments and fostering warm, responsive interactions can encourage children to seek assistance when facing challenges, thereby enhancing both emotional security and problem-solving capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Birch & Ladd, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, children's tendency to prioritize familiarity over immediate behavioral cues presents a double-edged pattern.
While familiarity can buffer against occasional negative interactions, persistent unresponsiveness from familiar teachers may normalize inadequate support.
This calls for teacher training programs to emphasize not only relationship-building but also the sustained provision of positive, consistent responsiveness over time (Rimm-Kaufman & Hamre, 2010).
text.formatted: This calls for teacher training programs to emphasize not only relationship-building but also the sustained provision of positive, consistent responsiveness over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Rimm-Kaufman & Hamre, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These insights are particularly relevant in educational situations with high teacher turnover or frequent exposure to unfamiliar caregivers, where relationship stability is fragile and children's access to reliable support may be compromised (LoCasale-Crouch et al., 2008).
text.formatted: These insights are particularly relevant in educational situations with high teacher turnover or frequent exposure to unfamiliar caregivers, where relationship stability is fragile and children's access to reliable support may be compromised <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(LoCasale-Crouch et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Intervention and policy efforts aimed at enhancing children's help-seeking competence should incorporate strategies that promote teacher stability, emotional attunement, and responsive caregiving.
Creating secure and consistent environments may help young children feel confident and safe when seeking help.
While this study provides new insights into how teachers' familiarity and response valence shape young children's help-seeking expectations, several questions remain.

First, previous studies on selective social learning have shown age-related changes in how children weigh relationship-related and behavioral cues (Corriveau & Harris, 2009; Corriveau et al., 2009; Williams & Danovitch, 2019).
text.formatted: First, previous studies on selective social learning have shown age-related changes in how children weigh relationship-related and behavioral cues <ref type="bibr">(Corriveau & Harris, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Corriveau et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Williams & Danovitch, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The current study's narrow age range limited the examination of such developmental differences.
Future research should adopt broader age spans to test how the integration of familiarity and response valence evolves across early childhood.
Second, the distinction between experience-based and knowledge-based familiarity warrants further investigation.
Direct interactional familiarity may rely on episodic memory and person-specific schemas, whereas verbally conveyed familiarity may depend on semantic processing and abstract social knowledge.
Future studies could combine neurocognitive measures (e.g., fNIRs or EEG) with behavioral paradigms to examine whether these forms of familiarity engage distinct cognitive and neural systems.

Third, although the third-party paradigm provided strong experimental control, it may not fully capture children's spontaneous help-seeking behaviors in real-world teacher-child interactions (Paulus & Caporaso, 2024).
text.formatted: Third, although the third-party paradigm provided strong experimental control, it may not fully capture children's spontaneous help-seeking behaviors in real-world teacher-child interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Paulus & Caporaso, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should incorporate naturalistic observations or interactive paradigms to examine whether experimentally observed patterns translate into daily behavior in authentic ECE settings.
In conclusion, the present study demonstrated that young children integrated both teachers' familiarity and response valence when forming help-seeking expectations.
Familiarity consistently emerged as the dominant cue, highlighting its foundational role in shaping children's representations of social support.

By revealing how young children flexibly coordinate relational and behavioral information, this work deepens our understanding of the social-cognitive mechanism of the formation of young children's help-seeking expectations and underscores the enduring importance of secure, responsive teacher-child relationships in early education.
